scenarios.title: Design for saved search alerts on a marketplace
scenarios.prompt:
The requirements for saved search alerts on our resale marketplace are approved. I need the design for the team that will build it. Nobody on that team was in the planning meetings, so they will work from what you write. The requirements and notes on what we already have are below.

Requirements

1. Saving a search
1.1 A signed-in buyer can save the current search filters under a name of 1 to 60 characters.
1.2 A buyer can have at most 20 saved searches. Trying to save a 21st is refused with a message that states the limit.
1.3 Two saved searches of the same buyer cannot have the same name.

2. Alerts
2.1 For each saved search with alerts on, the buyer gets at most one email per day listing the items that are new since the last email.
2.2 No email is sent on a day without new matches.
2.3 Every email has a link that turns alerts off for that saved search without signing in.

3. Managing
3.1 A buyer can rename, pause, resume or delete a saved search.
3.2 Only the buyer who owns a saved search can see or change it.
3.3 If a buyer changes the same saved search in two browser tabs at about the same time, the later save must not silently overwrite the earlier one.

4. Delivery problems
4.1 If the email service is unavailable, the alert is retried for up to 24 hours. After that it is dropped and counted in a metric.

5. Privacy
5.1 When a buyer deletes their account, all their saved searches are deleted within 24 hours.

What we already have
- Listings service (another team): publishes an event for every new item that is listed.
- Search service (another team): a query call that takes filters and a "since" time and returns matching items. Filters are category, maximum price and distance from a postcode.
- Email gateway (platform team): send(to, templateId, params). The provider allows 14 sends per second for our whole account and rejects sends above that with a "slow down" error.
- Shared sign-in check and shared logger from the platform library. Every handler already uses them.
- Accounts service: publishes an event when an account is deleted.
- Storage: one DynamoDB table for our app, with one secondary index that can be keyed by buyer.
- Compute: Lambda functions behind API Gateway. A scheduled rule can start a function once a day.
rubric: Every numbered requirement is tied to a named component, and the design says which requirements each covers, including the unsubscribe link (2.3) and the account deletion (5.1).
The saved search record lists each field with its type and constraints, including the name length limit, the name being unique per buyer, and which field identifies the owner.
Covers the case of two tabs saving the same saved search (3.3) and says how the later save finds out about the earlier one, for example a version check, and not only that overwriting must not happen.
Treats the email provider's send limit as a separate case from the email service being down, with its own handling.
For the email service being down, says what happens to the alert (retry window, then dropped and counted) and for the 21st saved search says what the buyer sees.
A developer could build the daily alert run from the design alone: it says what starts the run, how it finds the saved searches to process and how it knows what is new since the last email.
Opens with a summary of the feature, then covers the architecture, the components with their interfaces, the data structures, the error cases and the test approach, in that order.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: A realistic set of requirements in which some items have no obvious owner among the existing parts (the unsubscribe link that works without sign-in, the deletion on account closure) and the failure cases are spread across input, concurrency, an outside provider with a send limit, and an outage. The design has to map every requirement to a component (r01), give the stored record with field types and constraints (r05), cover the conflicting-save and throttling cases (r06) and say what the buyer or the alert does in each (r07), and be buildable by people who were not in the meetings (r10).

scenarios.title: Design for expiring share links to documents
scenarios.prompt:
Can you write the design for share links in our document app? The requirements are approved. The team that builds it is separate from the teams that own sign-in, the documents service and the CDN, so it should be clear what is ours and what is not.

Requirements

1. Creating a link
1.1 A document owner can create a share link with an expiry between 1 hour and 30 days.
1.2 Anyone with the link can view the document read-only until it expires, without signing in.
1.3 An owner can have at most 10 active links per document.

2. Revoking
2.1 An owner can revoke a link. After that the link no longer shows the document.
2.2 Revocation takes effect for every viewer within 10 seconds.

3. Viewing
3.1 A viewer who opens an expired or revoked link sees a page saying the link is no longer valid, with no hint of the document title.
3.2 A link to a deleted document shows the same page as an expired link.
3.3 Each view is counted, and the owner can see the count per link.

4. Access and limits
4.1 Only the document owner can create, list or revoke links for a document.
4.2 Viewing is limited to 60 requests per minute per link. A viewer above that sees a "try again later" page.

Notes on the existing system
- Sign-in: the platform team's shared check validates the session cookie and puts the user id on the request. It also refreshes sessions that are close to expiring and writes a sign-in audit record. All our handlers call it.
- Logging: the shared logger adds a correlation id and the user id to every line. We just call it.
- Documents service (another team): getDocument(documentId) returns the document or nothing, and getOwner(documentId) returns the owner's user id.
- Document bodies live in object storage and are served through a CDN. The CDN keeps bodies for 15 minutes. A cache purge by path reaches every edge location in up to 5 minutes.
- Our app has one DynamoDB table and Lambda functions behind API Gateway.
rubric: Says that the 10 second revocation (2.2) cannot be met with the CDN caching for 15 minutes, and proposes a change or asks for a decision rather than assuming it is met.
Calls the shared sign-in check, the shared logger and the documents lookup as existing parts, and does not restate their internals.
Gives the share link component's operations for creating, revoking, listing and opening a link, each with parameter types and a return type.
Treats a caller who is not the owner, an expiry outside the allowed range and a link to a deleted or unknown document as separate failure cases.
Describes checks in isolation, checks across components and end-to-end journeys as three separate groups, with concrete example cases such as an expired link and a revoked link.

Says how a link opened in a browser is identified and how it is decided to be expired, for example the token in the address and the stored expiry compared with the server time, so the viewing path can be built without asking.
Includes at least one diagram showing how a viewer's request moves through the CDN, the link component and the documents service.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: The system notes describe shared parts in enough detail to be tempting to restate (sign-in session refresh, audit record), and one requirement (revocation in 10 seconds) is in tension with the stated CDN behaviour. The design has to say that the requirement cannot be met as it stands (r02), keep to what the feature owns (r03), give typed operations (r04), cover separate failure cases (r06) and separate the test levels (r08), and be buildable without asking how expiry is decided (r10).

scenarios.title: Design for customer webhook delivery with retries
scenarios.prompt:
Please write the design for webhook delivery. The requirements are approved, and the engineers who will build it have asked for a design they can estimate from. Details of what we have to build on are below the requirements.

Requirements

1. Registering endpoints
1.1 A customer admin can register up to 5 endpoint URLs and choose which event types each one receives.
1.2 Only https URLs are accepted.
1.3 Each endpoint gets a signing secret that is shown once, when the endpoint is created.

2. Delivery
2.1 Each event is delivered at least once to every endpoint subscribed to its type, with a signature that the customer can verify.
2.2 The first attempt is made within 30 seconds of the event.
2.3 A response that is not a success, or no response within 10 seconds, counts as a failed attempt.
2.4 A failed attempt is retried with growing delays, up to 8 attempts over 24 hours.

3. Problem endpoints
3.1 After 8 failed attempts for one event, the endpoint is shown as failing.
3.2 If 50 events in a row fail for an endpoint, it is disabled and the admin is emailed.
3.3 An admin can re-enable a disabled endpoint and replay events from the last 7 days.

4. Visibility
4.1 An admin can see the last 100 delivery attempts for each endpoint, with outcome and response code.

What we can build on
- The orders and shipping services publish events to a shared event bus. Other teams' events will use the same bus later.
- A queue service with delayed delivery and a dead-letter queue is available. A scheduler that starts a function at a set time is also available.
- Outbound calls from our functions go through the platform's egress proxy.
- The platform's notification client sends email to an address.
- The shared sign-in check and logger are used by every handler.
- Storage: one DynamoDB table.
rubric: Gives the delivery component's operations, such as delivering an event to an endpoint, recording an attempt and re-enabling an endpoint, each with parameter and return types.
Treats a customer endpoint that times out or answers with an error as a failure case with its own handling, separate from an endpoint registered with a non-https URL.
For a failing endpoint, says what the admin sees at each stage (failing, disabled, the email) and that retries stop after the limit instead of continuing without end.

Separates checks in isolation, checks across components and end-to-end journeys, with concrete cases such as the retry schedule, a failed delivery reaching the dead-letter queue, and register-to-replay.
States what the design covers and what it leaves out, such as ordering between events, and gives a reason for the main design choice such as how retries are scheduled.
Says what is signed and how the customer verifies it, so the signature in 2.1 can be built from the design without asking.
Opens with a summary of the feature, then covers the architecture, the components with their interfaces, the data structures, the error cases and the test approach, in that order.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: The requirements leave real choices open (how retries are scheduled, whether events are ordered, how a failing endpoint is tracked) and the failures are the main subject. The design has to give typed operations (r04), separate the endpoint's failures from bad registrations (r06), say what the admin sees and when retries stop (r07), split the test levels (r08), say what is in and out of scope with a reason for the key choice (r09), and spell out the signature so it can be built (r10).

scenarios.title: Design for low-stock alerts on top of a nightly stock feed
scenarios.prompt:
We need the design for low-stock alerts for our merchandisers. The requirements were signed off last week. Please base the design on how our systems really work today; the notes are below.

Requirements

1. Thresholds
1.1 A merchandiser can set a reorder threshold for each product, from 0 to 10,000 units.
1.2 A product without a threshold uses a default of 10 units.

2. Alerts
2.1 When the stock of a product falls to or below its threshold, the merchandiser who owns its category gets an alert within 5 minutes of the stock change.
2.2 There is at most one open alert per product. No second alert is created while one is open.
2.3 An alert closes by itself when stock rises above the threshold.

3. Stock view
3.1 The merchandiser's product list shows the current stock of each product.
3.2 The stock shown is never more than 5 minutes old.

4. Access and records
4.1 A merchandiser sees only products in their own categories.
4.2 Every change of a threshold is written to the audit log with who changed it, when, the old value and the new value.

5. Reporting
5.1 Every Monday a summary lists the products that spent more than 2 days below their threshold in the previous week.

How stock works today
- Stock levels come from the warehouse system as one file every night, loaded into the inventory table at 02:00. There are no stock-change events. The warehouse team has a live feed on their roadmap with no date.
- The sales service publishes an order-placed event with product and quantity. Returns and warehouse corrections are not in any event.
- The catalog service (another team) owns products and categories, including which merchandiser owns each category.
- A shared audit client records who did what. A shared sign-in check and logger are used by every handler.
- The notification client sends email and in-app alerts.
- Compute: Lambda functions and a scheduler. Storage: one DynamoDB table plus the inventory table, which we read but do not own.
rubric: Every numbered requirement is tied to a named component and the design says which requirements each covers; the audit record of threshold changes (4.2) and the Monday summary (5.1) are covered and not left out.
Says that the 5 minute alert (2.1) and the 5 minute stock age (3.2) cannot be met with a nightly stock load, and offers a way forward or asks which way to go; it does not claim the figures are met.
Covers the nightly file not arriving or arriving incomplete, and the notification client failing, as failure cases with their own handling.
For a stock level that is late or missing, says what the merchandiser sees and what the system does about it, such as marking the figure as old.
Says what the design does and does not cover, for example not owning stock data, and gives a reason for the main choice such as estimating stock from order events or waiting for the live feed.

Says how an alert is opened and closed from a stock figure and a threshold, including when that is evaluated (on the nightly load, on events or on a schedule), so the rule can be built without asking.
Includes at least one diagram showing how stock figures, thresholds and alerts move between the components.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: Two requirements (5 minute alert, 5 minute stock age) cannot be met by a stock feed that updates once a night, and the notes say so without drawing the conclusion. Two others (audit of threshold changes, weekly summary) are easy to leave without a component. The design has to call out the conflict (r02), cover every requirement (r01), cover feed failure (r06) with a visible result (r07), say what it does not own and why it estimates or waits (r09), and define how the figures combine (r10).

scenarios.title: Design for organisation data export and deletion
scenarios.prompt:
Our admins have asked for a way to export and to delete their organisation's data, and the requirements for it are approved. Please write the design so the team can start building next sprint. What we have today is listed after the requirements.

Requirements

1. Export
1.1 An organisation admin can request an export of all the organisation's data.
1.2 The export is a zip of JSON files, ready within 24 hours of the request. The admin gets an email with a download link that works for 7 days.
1.3 An organisation can have only one export running at a time.

2. Deletion
2.1 An organisation admin can request deletion of the organisation. The request starts a 14 day waiting period in which any admin can cancel it.
2.2 When the waiting period ends, all the organisation's data is removed from the live systems within 24 hours.
2.3 Within the same 24 hours, every copy of the data, including backups, is removed.
2.4 When deletion is finished the admins get an email that gives the date it was completed.

3. Records
3.1 Each request, cancellation and completion is written to the audit log. Audit entries are kept for 7 years and contain no personal data once the organisation has been deleted.

4. Access
4.1 Only organisation admins can make these requests.
4.2 A request needs the admin to enter their password again.

What we have today
- The organisation's data is in three places: the main database (projects, tasks, members), the search index (a copy of task text) and object storage (attachments).
- The main database is snapshotted every night. Snapshots are kept for 35 days under the security team's compliance lock. Object storage keeps previous versions of attachments for the same 35 days.
- The audit log is a shared service with one call, record(actor, action, target, details). It is append-only.
- The shared sign-in check has reauthenticate(userId, password), which returns true or false.
- The notification client sends email.
- A workflow service can run a sequence of steps with waits and retries.
- Our own data lives in one DynamoDB table. Handlers are Lambda functions.
rubric: Says that requirement 2.3 (all copies removed in 24 hours) cannot be met while backups are locked for 35 days, and proposes a change or asks for a decision rather than assuming it is met.

Every numbered requirement is tied to a named component and the design says which requirements each covers; the audit retention rule (3.1) and the one-export-at-a-time rule (1.3) in particular have a named owner.
The request record lists each field with its type and constraints, including the kind of request, its state values, who made it and the timestamps that the waiting period depends on.
Covers a cancellation arriving when the deletion has already started, and a second export request while one is running, as conflict cases with a stated outcome.

Separates checks in isolation, checks across components and end-to-end journeys, with concrete cases such as a cancel inside the waiting period and a deletion that reaches the search index and the attachments.
Names every place the deletion has to reach (the main database, the search index and the attachments) so a developer knows the whole scope without asking.
Opens with a summary of the feature, then covers the architecture, the components with their interfaces, the data structures, the error cases and the test approach, in that order.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: One requirement (all copies, backups included, gone in 24 hours) collides with a fact mentioned in passing in the notes (locked 35 day snapshots), and two requirements (audit retention, one export at a time) belong to no obvious component. The design has to call out the backup conflict (r02), cover every requirement (r01), give the request record with constraints (r05), cover the concurrent cases (r06), separate the test levels (r08), and list every store the deletion reaches (r10).

scenarios.title: Design for bulk contact import
scenarios.prompt:
I need a design for importing contacts from a CSV file into our CRM. The requirements are approved. The notes after them describe the parts we get to use. Please write it so a developer who has not seen this feature before can build it.

Requirements

1. Upload
1.1 A user with permission to manage contacts can upload a CSV file of up to 50,000 rows and 20 MB to import contacts.
1.2 The email column is required. First name, last name, phone, company and tags are optional.
1.3 A row with an invalid email address is skipped and listed in an error report that the user can download.

2. Processing
2.1 The import runs in the background and the user can see how many rows have been processed.
2.2 A contact whose email already exists in the workspace is updated, not duplicated. Emails are compared in lower case.
2.3 A workspace can run only one import at a time.

3. Result
3.1 When the import ends, the user sees how many contacts were created, updated and skipped.
3.2 A user can cancel a running import. Rows already written stay.

4. Limits
4.1 An import may use at most half of the workspace's allowed contact writes, so the rest of the app keeps working.

The parts we get to use
- Contacts service (contacts team): upsertContacts(workspaceId, contacts) takes up to 100 contacts per call and returns a result for each one: created, updated, or rejected with a reason. When the workspace is over its write limit it answers "throttled" with a retry-after time in seconds. The limit is set per workspace in the contacts team's plan settings.
- File storage: the browser uploads straight to storage with a pre-signed address, and storage tells us when the upload is complete.
- A queue service and worker functions.
- A permission client: can(userId, workspaceId, permission) returns true or false.
- Shared sign-in check and logger. One DynamoDB table.
rubric: Gives the import component's operations, such as starting an import, reporting progress and cancelling, and the call it makes to the contacts service, each with parameter and return types.
The import job and the error report row list each field with type and constraints, such as the state values, the counts, the row number and the reason.
Treats the contacts service answering that the workspace is over its write limit as a failure case with its own handling, separate from a row that is rejected.
Covers a second import started while one is running (2.3) and a file over the row or size limit as failure cases with a stated response.
For the over-limit answer, says the worker waits and retries, and what the user sees meanwhile.
Says where the workspace's write limit comes from and how half of it is worked out and kept to, or states an assumption for it, so requirement 4.1 can be built without asking.
Includes at least one diagram showing how an upload becomes a finished import through storage, the queue, the worker and the contacts service.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: The import has one outside dependency that can push back (the contacts service with its write limit and retry time), a second kind of failure inside the file (bad rows, oversize), and a rule that depends on a number the notes do not state (half of the workspace limit). The design has to give typed operations (r04), the job and error row with constraints (r05), separate the throttling from the other failures (r06), say what happens and what the user sees (r07) and pin down where the limit comes from (r10).

scenarios.title: Design for comments on support tickets
scenarios.prompt:
Please write the design for comments on tickets in our helpdesk. The requirements are approved. Ticket management is a separate feature with its own design owned by another team; I have pasted what we need to know about it and the other shared parts.

Requirements

1. Adding comments
1.1 An agent who can access a ticket can add a comment of up to 10,000 characters.
1.2 A comment is public or internal. Internal comments are visible to agents only.
1.3 The customer who owns a ticket can add public comments through the portal.

2. Reading and editing
2.1 Comments appear oldest first with the author's name and the time.
2.2 The author can edit a comment within 15 minutes of posting. An edited comment shows that it was edited.
2.3 Comments cannot be deleted. An admin can redact a comment, which replaces its text with a notice and keeps the record.

3. Notifications
3.1 When an agent adds a public comment, the customer gets an email with the comment text.
3.2 When a comment mentions an agent with @ and their handle, that agent gets an in-app notification.

4. Rules
4.1 A closed ticket does not accept new comments.
4.2 Customers never see internal comments: not in the portal, not in emails and not in search results.

Existing parts
- Ticket management (its own design, other team) owns the ticket: ticket id, customer, team, assignee, status (open, pending, solved or closed), subject, priority, and the times it was created and last updated. It offers getTicket(ticketId), which returns the ticket or nothing, and canAccess(userId, ticketId), which returns true or false. It also owns every status change.
- The shared sign-in check validates the session, sets the user id and role (agent, admin or customer), refreshes sessions close to expiry and rate limits each user.
- The shared logger adds a correlation id to every line.
- Notification client: sendEmail(to, subject, body) and sendInApp(userId, message).
- User directory (other team): findByHandle(handle) returns a user id or nothing.
- Search (search team) indexes ticket text from a stream of our DynamoDB table. Its index settings take a list of attributes to leave out.
- Handlers are Lambda functions behind API Gateway.
rubric: Calls the ticket lookup, the access check and the other shared parts as existing parts, and does not restate the ticket's fields or their internals.
Every numbered requirement is tied to a named component, and hiding internal comments in the portal, emails and search (4.2) has a named owner.
The comment record lists each field with type and constraints, such as the length limit, the public or internal value, the posted and edited times, the redaction marker and the ticket it belongs to.
Treats a comment on a closed ticket, a comment by someone without access to the ticket and a comment over the length limit as separate failure cases.
Separates checks in isolation, checks across components and end-to-end journeys, with concrete cases such as an internal comment missing from the customer's view, the customer's email and search.
Says how the 15 minute edit window is decided, from which stored time and against which clock, so requirement 2.2 can be built without asking.
Opens with a summary of the feature, then covers the architecture, the components with their interfaces, the data structures, the error cases and the test approach, in that order.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: The notes give the ticket's full field list and the internals of the sign-in check, which invites restating them, while the requirement that customers never see internal comments reaches three places (portal, email, search) and the last one belongs to another team's index. The design has to refer to the owned parts and build on them (r03), give each requirement a named owner including the three hiding points (r01), define the comment record (r05), separate the failure cases (r06) and the test levels (r08), and say how the edit window is decided (r10).

scenarios.title: Design for redeeming loyalty points for vouchers
scenarios.prompt:
Here are the approved requirements for point redemption in our loyalty programme, followed by what the other teams provide. Please write the design for the team that will build the redemption part.

Requirements

1. Redeeming
1.1 A signed-in member can redeem points for a voucher worth £5 per 500 points, in multiples of 500, up to 5,000 points per day.
1.2 Points are deducted when the member redeems. The voucher code is shown once on screen and sent by email.
1.3 A balance can never go below zero, even if the member redeems from two devices at the same moment.

2. Problems
2.1 If the voucher cannot be issued after points were deducted, the points are restored within 1 minute.
2.2 A voucher code is 12 characters and unique.

3. History and support
3.1 A member can see their last 50 redemptions.
3.2 A support agent can reverse a redemption within 30 days. An unused voucher is voided. If the voucher was already used, the reversal is refused.

4. Limits
4.1 A member can make at most 5 redemption attempts per minute.

What the other teams provide
- Points ledger (loyalty-core team): getBalance(memberId) and applyChange(memberId, points, reason, requestKey). Writes are conditional. A request key that was used before returns the earlier result and does not apply the change again. Earning points, expiry of points and the balance screen belong to that team.
- Voucher service (payments team): issueVoucher(valueInPence, memberId) returns a voucher with its code. About 1 call in 200 times out, and a timed-out call may or may not have created the voucher. Also voidVoucher(code) and getVoucher(code), which returns unused, used or void.
- Notification client for email.
- Shared sign-in check with the roles member and support, and the shared logger.
- Handlers are Lambda functions. We have one DynamoDB table.
rubric: Covers two redemptions at the same moment (1.3) and says how the balance is kept from going below zero, for example with the ledger's conditional writes.
For the voucher service timing out after points were deducted, says what the member sees and whether the system retries, restores points or escalates, including the case where the voucher may exist.

States what the design covers and what it leaves out, such as earning and expiry of points, and gives a reason for the main choice, for example deducting first and restoring on failure rather than issuing first.
Calls the points ledger and the voucher service as existing parts; how balances and voucher codes are stored is not redesigned.
Separates checks in isolation, checks across components and end-to-end journeys, with concrete cases such as two simultaneous redemptions and a voucher timeout that restores the points.
Says how a redemption is identified so that a retry does not deduct points twice, for example what the request key is made from.
Includes at least one diagram showing the redemption flow between the member, the redemption component, the ledger and the voucher service, including the path when issuing fails.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: The money-like flow has three hard cases (two devices at once, a voucher call that times out after points were taken, a retry), two services owned by other teams, and scope that is easy to widen into earning and expiry. The design has to cover the concurrency (r06), say what the member sees and what the system does on a timeout (r07), state scope and the reason for deducting first (r09), build on the other teams' services (r03), separate the test levels (r08) and define the retry identity (r10).
